title: Production processes to achieve quantity and quality targets

lessons.title: Understanding quantity and quality targets
lessons.html:
What the nursery must deliver

Every nursery works to two kinds of targets. Quantity targets say how many plants of each kind must be produced, by when. Quality targets say how good those plants must be. Meeting one without the other is a failure: 5 000 poor shrubs cannot be sold, and 500 perfect ones cannot fill an order for 5 000.

Examples of quantity targets

  • 10 000 rooted cuttings of plumbago by the end of March.
  • 2 500 trays of bedding plants ready each week in spring.
  • 800 trees in 20-litre bags ready for a landscaping contract in November.
  • A daily rate, such as 3 000 bags potted by the team.

Examples of quality targets

  • Germination or strike rate of at least the level set by the manager.
  • Finished plant height and spread within the product specification.
  • Healthy white roots filling the container without circling badly.
  • No pests, diseases or weeds.
  • Correct labelling, clean containers.
  • Losses below the target percentage at each stage.

Where targets come from

Targets are set by management from customer orders, sales forecasts and the nursery's capacity. The supervisor helps to achieve them by planning daily work, organising the team and checking results. In this work-experience module you will take part in real production processes and show that you can help achieve both kinds of targets.

Allowing for losses

Because some plants are always lost, production starts with more units than the final target. If the nursery expects to lose 15% between sticking and sale, it must stick about 1 180 cuttings to finish with 1 000 good plants. Your loss records make these numbers more accurate over time.

lessons.title: Running production to hit the targets
lessons.html:
Turning plans into plants

Break the target down

Large targets are easier to manage when broken into weekly and daily amounts. A target of 10 000 cuttings in five weeks becomes 2 000 a week, or 400 a day over five working days. Write the daily target on the board and track it.

Control the key processes

ProcessWhat to control
PropagationClean material, correct technique, mist and temperature, labelling
PottingRight medium and container, correct depth, watering in
IrrigationEven coverage, right amount, early in the day
FeedingProgramme followed, EC and pH checked where used
Plant carePinching, spacing, staking, weeding on time
Pest controlWeekly scouting, early action, label-correct spraying by trained workers

Watch the crop

Walk the blocks every day. Look at colour, growth, roots (tip a few pots out), pests and dry spots. A crop that is slow or yellow needs attention now, not at dispatch. Report problems you cannot solve to the manager.

Use the team well

Put skilled workers on critical tasks, train others, and move people to where the work is behind. Keep the team informed about progress against target so they share in the effort and the success.

Safety

Production pressure must not override safety. Follow lifting procedures for heavy bags, keep machine guards in place and use protective equipment for chemicals and dust. Report any injury and make sure first aid is available from a trained first aider.

lessons.title: Measuring results and improving
lessons.html:
Knowing whether targets were met

Measure quantity

  • Count units completed each day and compare with the daily target.
  • Count stock in each block at set intervals.
  • Record germination and strike rates for every batch.
  • Record losses at each stage and the reason, such as damping-off, drought or frost.

Measure quality

  • Grade a sample of plants against the product standard before dispatch.
  • Record the percentage of top-grade, lower-grade and rejected plants.
  • Note customer complaints or returns.

Analyse the gap

When a target is missed, ask why. Was there a shortage of material, people or space? Was a technique applied incorrectly? Was the weather unusual? Did a pest get out of control? Use your records to find the real cause rather than guessing.

Take corrective action

Agree on actions with the manager, for example retraining the team, cleaning filters more often, changing the scouting day or starting a batch earlier next season. Then check whether the action worked.

Report clearly

Give the manager a short weekly report: target, actual, gap, reasons and actions. Keep it factual. Honest reports, even of bad results, help the nursery make better decisions.

Portfolio evidence

For this work-experience module collect evidence such as daily production sheets, batch records with strike rates, grading results, your weekly reports and your mentor's sign-off.

Key points

  • Quantity and quality targets must both be met.
  • Start with more units than the target to allow for losses.
  • Break targets into weekly and daily amounts and track them.
  • Control key processes and walk the crop daily.
  • Measure, find the real cause of gaps and agree corrective actions.
